sec.title: Background
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations represent the standard of care for advanced renal cell carcinoma. The OMNIVORE trial investigated a response-adaptive strategy, including treatment discontinuation in early nivolumab responders (Arm A) and salvage ipilimumab addition in non-responders (Arm B). Here we report outcomes with extended follow-up.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: OMNIVORE was a phase II response-adaptive trial in which patients received induction nivolumab monotherapy. Patients achieving a confirmed complete or partial response discontinued nivolumab and entered observation (Arm A), while patients with stable disease or progressive disease received two doses of ipilimumab added to ongoing nivolumab (Arm B). This analysis characterizes long-term overall survival across the full study cohort and durability of response among patients who discontinued nivolumab following an early objective response.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of 83 patients who initiated treatment, 12 (14%) were allocated to Arm A and 57 (69%) to Arm B, with a median follow-up among living patients of 59.4 months (range 29.1–85.4 months) in Arm A and 31.4 months (range 4.6–62.6 months) in Arm B. The 3-year overall survival rate from nivolumab initiation was 64% (95% CI 51% to 74%) in the overall cohort, 83% (95% CI 48% to 96%) in Arm A, and 63% (95% CI 47% to 76%) in Arm B. Of the 12 Arm A patients, 6 (50%) remained off nivolumab at 1 year following treatment discontinuation, of whom 5 maintained responses beyond 43 months off therapy, with all remaining alive at last known follow-up, with overall survival ranging from 48.8 to 85.4 months from nivolumab initiation. Of the six patients who resumed treatment, only one achieved a durable complete response remaining on treatment at 83.2 months from nivolumab initiation. All 57 Arm B patients discontinued treatment with a median treatment duration of 3.7 months (range 1–24.8 months) and a median progression-free survival from nivolumab plus ipilimumab initiation of 4.6 months (95% CI 2.7 to 6.5 months).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: With extended follow-up, a meaningful subset of patients achieving an early objective response to nivolumab maintained prolonged treatment-free survival following a short course of treatment. Salvage ipilimumab in nivolumab non-responders demonstrated limited benefit, reinforcing that upfront concurrent dual checkpoint blockade remains the preferred approach.
Keywords: Immunotherapy, Partial response, Kidney Cancer, Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor, Complete response - CR

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combinations are the established standard of care for advanced renal cell carcinoma, with long-term data from CheckMate 214 demonstrating durable survival and treatment-free survival benefits with nivolumab plus ipilimumab in a subset of patients.

With extended follow-up exceeding 5 years, 58% of patients achieving an early objective response to nivolumab monotherapy remained off treatment at 1 year, with several patients maintaining durable treatment-free survival beyond 4 years following a short course of therapy, while salvage ipilimumab in nivolumab non-responders continued to demonstrate limited benefit.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: These findings support the concept that prolonged immune checkpoint blockade exposure may not be necessary to achieve lasting tumor control in select responding patients, and highlight the need for prospective biomarker-driven randomized discontinuation trials to formally evaluate treatment discontinuation strategies in advanced renal cell carcinoma.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination regimens have transformed the treatment landscape for advanced renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and represent the current standard of care for patients with metastatic disease.1,4 Both immunotherapy combinations, such as nivolumab plus ipilimumab, and immunotherapy plus vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) combinations have demonstrated improved survival compared with sunitinib.1,4 The phase III CheckMate 214 trial was the first to establish dual immune checkpoint blockade as a frontline standard of care for patients with advanced RCC.3

With 9 years of follow-up, the longest reported for any phase III immune checkpoint inhibitor combination in this setting, nivolumab plus ipilimumab continued to demonstrate sustained and meaningful clinical benefit.5 6 Among patients with intermediate/poor-risk disease, overall survival (OS) remained superior with nivolumab plus ipilimumab compared with sunitinib (HR 0.69), with an objective response rate of 42%, a complete response rate of 12%, and a median duration of response of 82.8 months versus 19.8 months with sunitinib. Long-term exploratory analyses among patients with favorable-risk disease demonstrated a steadily improving OS HR over time (HR 0.80), and while the objective response rate was lower with nivolumab plus ipilimumab compared with sunitinib (30% vs 52%), patients achieved two times the rate of complete responses (13% vs 6%) and markedly more durable responses, with a median duration of response of 61.5 months versus 33.2 months with sunitinib, suggesting the potential for meaningful long-term benefit even in this population. Taken together, these data highlight that a meaningful subset of patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab derive deep and extended long-term benefit, underscoring the importance of characterizing outcomes with extended follow-up in this disease.

At the time of the design and initial reporting of CheckMate 214, many questions remained regarding the optimal use of immune checkpoint blockade in advanced RCC, including whether the benefits of immunotherapy could be maintained with less intensive treatment and whether sequential rather than upfront combination therapy could achieve comparable outcomes while reducing toxicity burden. It was in this context that the OMNIVORE trial, along with the TITAN RCC and HCRN GU16-260 trials, were designed to investigate a response-adaptive approach. In these trials, patients received induction nivolumab monotherapy with subsequent treatment allocation based on response to specifically investigate whether patients achieving an early response could safely discontinue treatment and maintain durable responses, and whether the addition of ipilimumab could rescue patients lacking a response to nivolumab.7,9 In the initial analysis of OMNIVORE with a median follow-up of 19.5 months, among patients who achieved an early response to nivolumab and discontinued treatment (n=12), 42% remained off therapy at 1 year after treatment discontinuation.9 However, among patients who did not respond to nivolumab and received salvage ipilimumab, the partial response or complete response conversion rate was only 4% with no complete responses observed. To better characterize the activity of salvage nivolumab plus ipilimumab after nivolumab monotherapy across these three trials, we performed a pooled analysis including 410 patients with advanced clear cell RCC.10 The objective response rate to salvage nivolumab plus ipilimumab was 12.6%, with a 3-year OS of 59% from nivolumab initiation, collectively confirming that sequential rather than concomitant delivery of dual checkpoint blockade yields limited benefit.

Notably, while the pooled analysis and the TITAN RCC and HCRN GU16-260 trials focused on the question of salvage ipilimumab in nivolumab non-responders, neither trial incorporated a prospectively defined treatment discontinuation arm for patients achieving an early objective response to nivolumab. This represents a novel aspect of the OMNIVORE trial design, and the durability of response following early nivolumab discontinuation in patients achieving an objective response remains a clinically relevant question in the context of treatment-free survival as an emerging endpoint in advanced RCC.11 12 Although anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) therapy is typically given for up to 2 years in currently approved combination regimens for advanced RCC, the optimal duration of immunotherapy in the context of favorable treatment response remains uncertain. Herein, we present long-term outcomes from the OMNIVORE trial (NCT03203473) with extended follow-up, providing updated survival outcomes and characterizing the durability of response following nivolumab discontinuation in early responders.

sec.title: Patient population
sec.p: The full eligibility criteria and trial methodology for the OMNIVORE study have been previously reported.9 In brief, eligible patients had histologically confirmed advanced RCC of any histologic subtype, with advanced disease defined as unresectable, locally recurrent, or metastatic. Prior systemic therapy was permitted with the exception of prior PD-1 pathway or cytotoxic T-lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) inhibitor exposure. Patients were required to have measurable disease per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors V.1.1 (RECIST V.1.1), an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 2 or less, and adequate organ function. A history of autoimmune disease necessitating systemic immunosuppression was exclusionary. This study was sponsored by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (DFCI). The protocol was approved by the institutional review board at the DFCI (Protocol Number 17–064) and each participating institution. All patients provided written informed consent prior to any study-related procedures. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: OMNIVORE was a multicenter phase II response-adaptive trial in which all patients received induction nivolumab monotherapy, with subsequent treatment allocation determined by radiographic response per RECIST V.1.1 within the first 6 months of therapy. Patients achieving a confirmed objective response, defined as a partial response or complete response, discontinued nivolumab and entered a period of active observation (Arm A). On disease progression, nivolumab was reinitiated, and ipilimumab was added if progression persisted or recurred. Patients who did not achieve an objective response, defined as confirmed stable disease or progressive disease, received the addition of two doses of ipilimumab to ongoing nivolumab (Arm B). Combination therapy was administered as nivolumab 3 mg/kg and ipilimumab 1 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks for two doses. Radiographic response assessments were performed at regular intervals throughout the study as previously described.

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: The primary objectives of the trial were to determine the proportion of Arm A patients maintaining a durable response, defined as the absence of disease progression and treatment-free at 1 year following nivolumab discontinuation, and to determine the proportion of Arm B patients achieving a confirmed objective response following the addition of ipilimumab. The key secondary endpoints included OS, defined as the time from nivolumab initiation to death from any cause; treatment-free interval, defined as the time from discontinuation of nivolumab therapy to the initiation of subsequent systemic therapy (either nivolumab alone or nivolumab in combination with ipilimumab, Arm A only); progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the time from nivolumab and ipilimumab initiation to radiographic disease progression or death from any cause (Arm B only). The present analysis reports long-term outcomes with extended follow-up, with a focus on OS across the full study cohort, durability of response among patients who discontinued nivolumab following an early objective response, and characterization of the subset of patients deriving prolonged clinical benefit.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The statistical design of the original trial has been previously described in detail. Median follow-up was estimated among living patients. Kaplan-Meier methodology was used to estimate distributions of OS (for the overall cohort and by treatment arm) and PFS (for Arm B). The proportion of Arm A patients remaining off nivolumab at 1 year after treatment discontinuation is reported with 90% two-sided exact binomial CIs. Swimmer plot and individual patient data listing are used to summarize baseline patient characteristics and treatment outcomes for Arm A patients.

sec.title: Patient disposition and baseline characteristics
sec.p: Baseline patient and disease characteristics have been previously described in detail.9 Briefly, 83 patients initiated treatment across 10 US centers, the majority of whom were male (82%), had good performance status (99% with ECOG performance status 0–1), and had International Metastatic Renal Cell Carcinoma Database Consortium (IMDC) intermediate or poor risk disease (67%). Clear cell histology was present in 96% of patients, and approximately half of patients (51%) were treatment-naive.

Of the 83 patients who initiated treatment, 69 (83%) underwent arm allocation: 12 patients (14%) were allocated to Arm A and 57 patients (69%) were allocated to Arm B (figure 1). 14 of the 83 patients (17%) did not undergo arm allocation due to progressive disease (n=7) or toxicity (n=7). Baseline characteristics by arm allocation are summarized in table 1. Compared with Arm B patients, Arm A patients were more frequently treatment-naive (58% vs 44%), had a higher rate of prior nephrectomy (100% vs 89%), and more frequently had rhabdoid differentiation (33% vs 11%). IMDC risk distribution was similar between arms, with favorable risk in 33% of Arm A and 39% of Arm B patients, and intermediate risk in 58% and 51%, respectively. Sarcomatoid differentiation was present in 17% of Arm A and 7% of Arm B patients.

sec.title: Patient follow-up
sec.p: With a database lock of April 28, 2025, the median follow-up among living patients from nivolumab initiation was 32.2 months (range 4.6–85.4 months) for the overall cohort. Median follow-up was longest among Arm A patients at 59.4 months (range 29.1–85.4 months), compared with 31.4 months (range 4.6–62.6 months) in Arm B patients and 27.4 months (range 24.3–33.1 months) in patients without an arm assignment.

sec.title: Overall survival
sec.p: At the time of analysis, 31 deaths were observed across the full cohort. The 3-year OS rate from nivolumab initiation was 64% (95% CI 51% to 74%) for the overall cohort (figure 2A). OS was notably higher among Arm A patients (figure 2B), with a 3-year OS rate of 83% (95% CI 48% to 96%), compared with 63% (95% CI 47% to 76%) in Arm B patients (figure 2C).

caption.title: Overall survival from nivolumab initiation. Kaplan-Meier estimates of overall survival from nivolumab initiation for (A) the overall cohort, (B) patients allocated to Arm A, and (C) patients allocated to Arm B. The 3-year overall survival rate was 64% (95% CI 51% to 74%) in the overall cohort, 83% (95% CI 48% to 96%) in Arm A, and 63% (95% CI 47% to 76%) in Arm B. Tick marks indicate censored observations.

sec.title: Arm A outcomes
sec.p: Among the 12 patients allocated to Arm A, 6 patients (50%, 90% CI 25% to 75%) remained off nivolumab at 1 year following treatment discontinuation (figure 3 and online supplemental table 1: Subjects 1–6). Of these, five patients maintained responses beyond 43 months off nivolumab with observation periods ranging from 43.8 to 58.2 months, and all alive at last known follow-up with OS ranging from 48.8 to 85.4 months from nivolumab initiation. One patient allocated to Arm A with stable disease remained treatment-free at 1 year after discontinuing nivolumab, but subsequently progressed and restarted nivolumab monotherapy after 20 months of observation. He later discontinued nivolumab due to toxicity.

caption.title: Swimmer plot of Arm A treatment and outcomes. Each bar represents an individual patient allocated to Arm A and depicts the duration and sequence of treatment. Time is measured in months from nivolumab initiation. Bar length reflects the duration of protocol treatments or survival follow-up. Complete response, progression and survival status are indicated for each patient. Subjects 1–6 remained treatment-free at 1-year following nivolumab discontinuation.

sec.p: Six patients allocated to Arm A experienced progression or reinitiated nivolumab within 1-year following nivolumab discontinuation (figure 3 and online supplemental table 1: Subjects 7–12). Of note, one patient reinitiated nivolumab while still in partial response within 1 year of treatment initiation during the observation period, representing a protocol violation, and subsequently achieved a complete response, remaining on treatment at 83.2 months from nivolumab initiation. One patient experienced progression at 11 months after discontinuing nivolumab and withdrew from protocol treatment. Among the remaining four patients who did not maintain durable responses off nivolumab, one reinitiated nivolumab monotherapy but subsequently discontinued due to toxicity, and three subsequently received nivolumab plus ipilimumab with limited benefit with no patient demonstrating a response to treatment.

At the time of data cut-off, three Arm A patients had died and nine remained alive, highlighting that a meaningful subset of patients achieving an early objective response to nivolumab can maintain prolonged treatment-free survival following treatment discontinuation. Figure 4 displayed the maximum decline in tumor size during study treatment for 12 patients in Arm A.

Waterfall plot depicting the maximum per cent change in target lesion size from baseline among patients allocated to Arm A (n=12). Each bar represents an individual patient. Blue bars indicate treatment-naïve patients; red bars indicate previously treated patients. The dashed horizontal line denotes the –30% threshold for partial response per the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors V.1.1. Patients are ordered by depth of response.

sec.title: Arm B outcomes
sec.p: All 57 patients allocated to Arm B discontinued treatment, with a median treatment duration of 3.7 months (range 1–24.8 months). The last on-study disease assessment in Arm B was February 22, 2021, with 44 PFS events reported. Among the 13 patients who did not experience progression, treatment discontinuation was due to toxicity (n=8), physician decision (n=4) and intercurrent illness (n=1). 7 of the 13 patients had stable disease at last assessment, with three maintaining disease control for more than 9 months (range 1.5–21.2 months). Six patients discontinued prior to the first scheduled imaging assessment. Median PFS from the initiation of nivolumab plus ipilimumab was 4.6 months (95% CI 2.7 to 6.5 months, figure 5). At the time of data cut-off, 21 deaths had been observed in Arm B.

caption.title: Progression-free survival from nivolumab plus ipilimumab initiation in Arm B. Kaplan-Meier estimate of progression-free survival from the initiation of nivolumab plus ipilimumab for patients allocated to Arm B (n=57). Median progression-free survival was 4.6 months (95% CI 2.7 to 6.5 months). Tick marks indicate censored observations.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The OMNIVORE trial was designed to address two clinically important questions in the management of advanced RCC: whether nivolumab could be safely discontinued in patients achieving an early objective response, and whether the sequential addition of ipilimumab could rescue patients failing to respond to nivolumab monotherapy. In the initial analysis, 42% of patients in Arm A maintained treatment-free status at 1 year following nivolumab discontinuation, while the partial response or complete response conversion rate with salvage ipilimumab in Arm B was only 4% with no complete responses observed.9 With extended follow-up now exceeding 5 years in responding patients, we report that 50% of Arm A patients remained off nivolumab at 1 year following treatment discontinuation, with five of these patients maintaining responses beyond 43 months off therapy. These long-term data support the hypothesis that a meaningful subset of patients achieving an early objective response to nivolumab can sustain prolonged treatment-free survival following discontinuation, while reinforcing that sequential rather than upfront dual checkpoint blockade yields limited clinical benefit.

The concept of treatment discontinuation in responding patients is increasingly relevant in the context of the long-term follow-up data from CheckMate 214.5 12 With 9 years of follow-up, nivolumab plus ipilimumab continued to demonstrate durable survival and response benefits over sunitinib.5 Notably, among the 12% of patients in CheckMate 214 who achieved a complete response with nivolumab plus ipilimumab, 62% discontinued therapy and have not initiated subsequent systemic treatment, underscoring the potential for enduring treatment-free survival in deep responders. Treatment-free survival, defined as the time between cessation of immunotherapy and the start of subsequent therapy, has emerged as an important endpoint in advanced RCC to characterize the period of ongoing benefit patients experience after stopping treatment.12 In the CheckMate 214 trial, treatment-free survival analyses have demonstrated that a meaningful proportion of patients treated with nivolumab plus ipilimumab experience sustained periods off therapy without disease progression, particularly among those achieving deep responses, highlighting the unique capacity of dual checkpoint blockade to induce durable immune-mediated tumor control beyond the period of active treatment. The OMNIVORE data extend this observation to patients treated with nivolumab monotherapy, demonstrating that a short course of nivolumab administered for 4–6 months can induce durable treatment-free survival beyond 4 years in a meaningful subset of patients, suggesting that prolonged exposure to immune checkpoint blockade may not be necessary to achieve lasting immune-mediated tumor control.

Although correlative data from OMNIVORE are pending, several lines of translational evidence inform the biological basis of durable treatment-free survival following a short course of PD-1 blockade. First, foundational work from Im and colleagues identified a PD-1+CD8+ T-cell population with stem-like properties, capable of self-renewal and giving rise to terminally differentiated effector cells, with the proliferative burst following PD-1 blockade arising almost exclusively from this TCF1-dependent subset.13 Second, work from Siddiqui and colleagues extended these observations to the tumor microenvironment, identifying an analogous intratumoral Tcf1+PD-1+CD8+ T-cell population that mediates the proliferative response to checkpoint blockade and gives rise to both self-renewing progenitors and differentiated effector progeny, with ablation of this subset abrogating responses to immunotherapy.14 Third, Ribas and colleagues demonstrated in patients with metastatic melanoma that PD-1 blockade expands intratumoral memory T-cell populations, with responders developing persistent expansion of tumor-reactive T-cell clones detectable long after treatment.15 Together, these data support a model in which the durability of benefit from PD-1 blockade depends not on continuous drug exposure, but on the successful expansion and ongoing self-renewal of a stem-like progenitor pool established during the initial period of treatment, with the resulting effector and memory progeny providing the cellular substrate for sustained tumor control after drug withdrawal.

Beyond this progenitor-effector framework, the broader composition and functional state of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes are critical determinants of response durability. Tumors enriched with antigen-experienced but non-terminally exhausted CD8+T cells may retain the capacity for reinvigoration on PD-1 blockade and may sustain immune-mediated tumor control after treatment withdrawal, while tumors with high infiltration of PD-1-expressing regulatory T cells are associated with resistance. Work from our collaborative group demonstrated that clonal neoantigen load was significantly higher in exceptional responders to dual checkpoint blockade compared with intermediate responders and those with progressive disease in the CheckMate 214 cohort, and was an independent predictor of PFS in multivariable analysis, while traditional markers including tumor mutational burden, frameshift mutation burden, and genomic instability did not associate with exceptional response.16 Notably, this association was specific to the exceptional response phenotype and was not observed when comparing all objective responders against non-responders, suggesting that the molecular determinants of durable treatment-free survival may be distinct from those driving initial response. Collectively, durable treatment-free survival likely reflects a confluence of tumor-intrinsic immunogenic features and a favorable immune microenvironmental context rather than any single determinant.

The low rate of response conversion with salvage ipilimumab in Arm B of OMNIVORE is consistent with data from the pooled analysis of OMNIVORE, TITAN RCC, and HCRN GU16-260 trials, which demonstrated an objective response rate of only 12.6% with salvage nivolumab plus ipilimumab in nivolumab non-responders.7,10 These findings are further supported by the FRACTION-RCC trial, which evaluated nivolumab plus ipilimumab in patients with advanced clear cell RCC who had progressed on prior immunotherapy.17 Among 46 patients with a median follow-up of 33.8 months, the objective response rate was 17.4%, with a median duration of response of 16.4 months and a median OS of 23.8 months. The role of CTLA-4 blockade in the post-immunotherapy setting was further evaluated in the KEYMAKER-U03 substudy 03B, a phase I/II platform trial enrolling patients with advanced clear cell RCC who had progressed on prior programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-(L)1) inhibitor and VEGF-TKI therapy.18 In the pembrolizumab plus quavonlimab arm, the objective response rate was 30.0% (95% CI 11.9% to 54.3%) with no complete responses, a median PFS of 5.4 months (95% CI 1.5 to 17.8), and a median duration of response that was not reached. While a subset of patients derived durable benefit, these data collectively confirm that the addition of CTLA-4 blockade following progression on or failure to respond to PD-1 inhibition yields modest response rates, and that upfront concurrent dual checkpoint blockade remains the preferred approach.

The OMNIVORE data do not directly address the question of immunotherapy rechallenge in patients progressing after adjuvant pembrolizumab, as patients enrolled in Arm B were progressing on active nivolumab therapy. Whether dual checkpoint blockade has meaningful activity in patients relapsing after adjuvant PD-1 inhibition remains an open question and the timing of relapse relative to adjuvant therapy completion is likely an important determinant of rechallenge benefit. The Advanced Urologic Cancer Consensus Conference highlighted support for immunotherapy rechallenge in appropriately selected patients, with preference for rechallenge increasing with longer intervals from adjuvant pembrolizumab completion, reflecting the view that later relapse may be more amenable to rechallenge than early progression.19 Prospective data in this population are needed.

Understanding the biology of response and resistance to immune checkpoint blockade in advanced RCC remains a critical and unmet need. The identification of validated predictive biomarkers spanning tissue-based molecular signatures, tumor immunologic features, and blood-based circulating markers, would meaningfully inform treatment discontinuation decisions and patient selection for salvage strategies.1620,25 Transcriptomic profiling from the IMmotion150 and IMmotion151 trials has demonstrated that patients with tumors demonstrating high T-effector gene expression signatures benefited preferentially from immunotherapy-based regimens, while those with high angiogenesis gene expression derived greater benefit from sunitinib, providing a molecular framework for understanding the heterogeneity of response observed in OMNIVORE.22 24 At the genomic and clonal level, work from Braun, Signoretti, and colleagues has shown that a high clonal neoantigen load is a specific determinant of exceptional response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.16 From an immunologic standpoint, tumors enriched with antigen-experienced but not terminally exhausted CD8+T cells are more likely to derive benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors, while tumors enriched with PD-1-expressing regulatory T cells are more likely to be resistant. These features that may account for the spectrum of outcomes observed across OMNIVORE arms.21 25 In the blood-based biomarker space, circulating kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), a transmembrane protein overexpressed in clear cell RCC, has emerged as a promising minimally invasive early predictor of immunotherapy response.23 In a post hoc analysis of CheckMate 214, patients with a greater than 30% decrease in KIM-1 at 3 weeks after the first dose of nivolumab plus ipilimumab had a median PFS of 70.8 months, a median OS of 85.4 months, and an overall response rate of 69.3%. In contrast, patients with a greater than 30% increase in KIM-1 at 3 weeks had a median PFS of 4.2 months, a median OS of 26.6 months, and an overall response rate of 13.9%. Taken together, these findings suggest that early KIM-1 kinetics could serve as a clinically actionable tool to identify patients most likely to achieve durable benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy and may guide treatment discontinuation decisions.

The OMNIVORE trial prospectively incorporated mandatory pretreatment biopsies, serial circulating-free DNA (cfDNA) and circulating tumor cells collections, and a single-cell sequencing cohort specifically designed to evaluate mechanisms of durable response and resistance. Completion of these analyses will be essential for characterizing the immunogenomic correlates of durable treatment-free survival in Arm A and resistance to salvage ipilimumab in Arm B. T-effector gene expression profiling, clonal neoantigen burden, CD8+T cell exhaustion states, and serial cfDNA and KIM-1 kinetics during the observation period represent the highest-priority analyses to yield mechanistic insight and inform future prospective biomarker-driven discontinuation trials. It is likely that a multimodal approach integrating tumor-intrinsic genomic features and immune microenvironment context will likely be required to prospectively identify patients most suitable for this strategy. Circulating biomarkers including KIM-1 kinetics and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) are promising but require prospective validation. Embedding these analyses within future randomized trials will be essential before clinical application. Collectively, these molecular, immunologic, and circulating biomarker data underscore the importance of prospective correlative studies in future trials evaluating treatment discontinuation strategies in advanced RCC.

This analysis has several limitations. The small number of patients allocated to Arm A precludes definitive conclusions about the durability of response following nivolumab discontinuation, and the lack of a randomized comparator arm limits the ability to attribute outcomes directly to the treatment discontinuation strategy. A proportion of Arm A patients withdrew from follow-up, and their subsequent outcomes are unknown, potentially affecting the interpretation of long-term results. Additionally, baseline tissue biomarker analyses from OMNIVORE, including PD-L1 expression and CD8+tumor infiltrating lymphocyte status, remain under investigation and may provide further insight into the characteristics of patients who achieved durable treatment-free survival. While the published literature provides a biological rationale for the durable responses observed in Arm A, dedicated mechanistic data from the OMNIVORE cohort are needed to formally characterize the immunogenomic correlates of durable treatment-free survival, and completion of the prospectively planned correlative analyses remains a high priority. Finally, the treatment landscape for advanced RCC has evolved substantially since OMNIVORE was designed, with multiple immunotherapy-based combinations now established as frontline standards of care, and the question of treatment discontinuation in responding patients remains most relevant in the context of these combination regimens.

In summary, with extended follow-up from the OMNIVORE trial, we demonstrate that a meaningful subset of patients achieving an early objective response to nivolumab monotherapy can maintain prolonged treatment-free survival following a short course of treatment, with several patients remaining off therapy beyond 4 years. These long-term data are hypothesis-generating and support the concept that durable treatment-free survival is achievable in select patients, though the small sample size and non-randomized design preclude definitive conclusions. How to prospectively identify patients most likely to sustain durable treatment-free survival following nivolumab discontinuation remains an open question. Prospective biomarker studies will be essential for advancing this concept and for rationally selecting patients in whom treatment can be safely stopped. Salvage ipilimumab in nivolumab non-responders continues to demonstrate limited benefit, consistent with the prior pooled analysis and the broader literature on sequential immune checkpoint blockade. Prospective biomarker studies identifying the immunogenomic and circulating correlates of exceptional and durable response will be essential for rationally selecting patients for treatment discontinuation strategies and for optimizing the use of immune checkpoint blockade in advanced RCC.

Ethics approval: This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the Dana Farber Cancer Institute and participating institutions. Participants gave informed consent to participate in the study before taking part.

Data availability free text: The OMNIVORE trial (NCT03203473) was an investigator-initiated, multicenter phase II trial. De-identified individual participant data that underlie the results reported in this article, along with the study protocol and statistical analysis plan, will be made available to qualified investigators for methodologically sound research proposals beginning 12 months after publication. All requests will be reviewed by the study leadership to ensure the proposed use is consistent with the informed consent provided by trial participants, that the research is for a legitimate scientific purpose, and that appropriate data protections are in place. A signed data access agreement will be required before any data are released.
